# v1.1.0-dev.79 — Zones you can snap to, dialogs that fit, windows that fold

Pre-release off the `dev` branch. Builds on `v1.1.0-dev.78`.

## Your FancyZones Zones, In The Visual Editor

Turn on FancyZones in the visual editor and it draws the zones PowerToys
would snap a window into. Drag a window onto one and it lands on that
zone exactly. A picker overrides which layout is drawn, and the default
is whatever FancyZones itself has applied to that monitor.

This reads PowerToys' config and never writes to it. Those files are
live: PowerToys holds them in memory and rewrites them on its own
schedule, so writing there would race it and could lose the layouts you
built. Zone authoring stays in PowerToys' own editor.

Monitors are keyed the way FancyZones keys them, by the PnP hardware id,
with the device instance breaking ties between two identical panels.
Profiles save that alongside the geometry now. Profiles saved before
this borrow it from the live monitor in the same role, so zones still
resolve, and they pick up the stored value on their next save.

Custom grids and canvases, and the columns, rows and grid templates, are
computed exactly. `priority-grid` is a table PowerToys keeps internally.
The shapes reproduced with confidence are 1, 2 and 3 zones. Anything
larger falls back to an even grid and says it is approximate rather than
drawing a guess as though it were the real thing.

Snapping goes by how much of the window covers a zone rather than by how
close its corners are. Dragging a window mostly over a zone is the
gesture, and a quarter of the window reads as intent without demanding
precision. Brushing an edge doesn't snap.

## Windows Fold Down To Reach What's Behind

A window sitting on top of another hid it completely. The "+N" badge
said something was under there and clicking cycled through them, but
there was no way to move the top one aside and work on what was behind.

Every window has a collapse control now that folds it to its title row,
and the legend carries a Collapse overlapping / Expand all toggle that
acts on the windows actually covering something rather than everything
on the canvas.

Collapsed windows in the same stack cascade instead of stacking. Two
windows saved at the same spot fold to two bars at the same spot, and
the upper one would hide the lower one exactly as the full-size window
did, which is the problem this is meant to solve.

None of it touches your layout. A collapsed window still loads at its
full saved size.

## A Window Can Say How It Should Be Recognised

Apps rewrite their titles as you work. An editor names the file you have
open, a browser names the page. A window saved with an exact title stops
being found the moment it says something else, and the matcher drops to
a weaker test that can pick the wrong window of the same app.

The window editor now lets each window choose:

- **App and its exact title**, which is what it has always done
- **App and a title starting with…**, for the part that stays put
- **App and window type, any title**, for apps that rename constantly

Giving up the title gives up an identity, so both looser modes require
the window class and kind to match instead. An explicit rule also binds
the process-only fallback: if you wrote "starts with Inbox" you were
being selective on purpose, and handing you any window of the app would
undo the rule you just wrote.

The pattern box seeds from the stable tail of the saved title, so
"main.js - WLM - Visual Studio Code" offers "Visual Studio Code" rather
than the filename that changes.

## Dialogs Fit What They Hold

The window editor flowed eight fields across two columns, which put X
beside State and Y beside Width. X and Y now pair together, W and H
pair together, each on a row of its own, and Colour moved up beside
State. The dialog comes out 560x428 instead of 1010x368.

Three separate things had been keeping dialogs the wrong size:

- **Best fit could grow a dialog but never shrink one.** A dialog's
  content box is the full height of its window, so the measurement could
  only ever report the window's own height back at it. The editor sat at
  its floor with an empty band under the fields because of that.
- **A scrollbar that changed the layout.** Measuring unlocks the
  scrollers, which takes their scrollbars away, which makes them wider,
  which reflows the content shorter. Best fit then applied a height only
  reachable without a scrollbar, which brought the scrollbar straight
  back. The display editor settled 4px short with its body scrolling
  under a window 6px below the size it was allowed to grow to.
- **A pass budget spent on measurements rather than resizes.** Dialogs
  that fill themselves from IPC report several times, and those no-op
  passes ran the budget out before the real correction landed. Dialogs
  re-measure when their own content changes now, which is what the
  display editor needed: its monitor modes arrive late and changed no
  size, so nothing measured it again.

The display editor also lost the empty space that was pushing it over.
A trailing section margin, and the last monitor card's bottom margin
collapsing through two parents onto the scroll container, were 34px of
nothing under the final card.

History opens 25% narrower and 25% taller. Fitted to its content it came
out 1072x462, which is the wrong shape for a list of runs.

## Companion Software Knows What It Found

The tab used to block on a single registry sweep before it drew
anything, so opening it looked like the app had hung. It paints every
row from the catalog first and fills in what it learned after: rows at
4ms, detection about 700ms later. Nothing is cached, because a cached
answer goes stale the moment you install something.

Detection also matched on names alone, which found things but couldn't
say which version or offer to remove them. It reads the uninstall
registry properly now and reports a version, a quiet uninstall command
where one exists, plus two fallbacks for software that never registers
there: installed drivers via pnputil, and executables on PATH. That last
one is what lets PowerShell 7 register as present.

**Parsec joins the catalog.** Its privacy-mode virtual displays are
exactly the thing that reshuffles your windows, which is the case WLM
was written for. It ships three registry entries whose names all begin
with "Parsec", so the entry excludes its own drivers rather than
claiming to be installed on the strength of one sitting beside it.

## Settings Gets Window And About Tabs

Reset window positions moved to a **Window** tab of its own, which left
Diagnostics short enough to stop scrolling. **About** became a tab
rather than a footnote under Updates, and it shows the running version
and where your profiles live.

## Install

Auto-updates from dev.53 and later. Otherwise unzip and run.
